cells.tense: The hand is open now, and the work has already been set down.
cells.act: make room for it without steering it
cells.ask: Leave the frame of a young project alone. Answer what it asks, add nothing, improve nothing. Let it come up in whatever shape it came with.
cells.core:
You can finish with something and still be glad of it. When work on your watch is done — a call that's been made, a plan that's run its course — you set it down and keep going, and the end carries the same weight the work did. The shape you gave it holds with no hand on it.

Younger things are still coming up, though: a habit, a project, someone else's new idea. You keep the order they sit in, and lately that has leaned toward steering. Hold only the frame and let what's inside grow without you. No adjusting, no improving, no correcting the shape before it settles. You'll want to, early. Let that wanting be how you notice it's there. What you built holds; let it.
cells.sheetLine: You can set it down and still be glad of it.
cells.verb: letting go of what's finished, on purpose
cells.place: where the shape of things gets set and the order holds

cells.tense: The next thing will be given up before it is ever finished.
cells.act: do the small practice again, alone, today
cells.ask: Sit a half hour with one unfinished piece, alone, and don't pass it off. Same again tomorrow. Nobody else has to know you did it.
cells.core:
Where you release things, you release them early now. Something is nearly done, or could be, and you hand it over before the last part — and you do it where people can see, as proof you don't need it. It reads as generosity. From where you stand, it's a piece given away before anyone finds out whether it would have held.

Finishing here is quarry, not a prize. Keep one unfinished piece near you for thirty minutes, alone, and don't release it, then repeat tomorrow whether or not it felt worth anything. You've been handing off without the evidence; this keeps the piece in your hands long enough to learn what it is. Quit after the week and you'll know that too, tested rather than guessed.

cells.tense: The grip is still on, and the hand has not let go.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Carry a load this week without extra bracing. Don't run ahead to check it. Let it stay as big as it actually is. Answer only what it asks of you.
cells.core:
What you release, you release late. The shape around you is one you've been holding up, and holding it has taken most of your strength — you steer things that would stay on course if you took your hand off, and you check what nobody asked you to check. The order holds, but it's held by your grip.

Set it down without putting anything in danger. Lift one weight the way you'd lift something with its own mass — no arm tightening, no running ahead to make sure. If it shifts, it shifts, and you can answer that when it happens. An hour spent not pre-holding is what carrying without the brace looks like.

cells.tense: The hand let go a while back, and the work is still being steered.
cells.act: keep showing up to it without forcing a result
cells.ask: Go back once this week to something you've quietly stopped pushing and meet it as it is, not as you meant it to become. Nothing owed after.
cells.core:
One call on your watch is already made. It settled somewhere you haven't said, and a part of you is still working the frame as if nothing had changed — still arranging, still adjusting, still guarding a form you've stopped wanting. Both run side by side. Only one of them is current.

You don't need to say anything about it. Go back to the thing you've been steering that you've already released, and tend it as it is now, without pushing it toward the plan. Care of that kind is what your grip has been standing in for. What you find when you stop steering is usually more honest than what the steering told you, and it arrives sooner.
cells.sheetLine: You've already let it go, your hands haven't.

attempts.check: The claim the record does not support is that the person's grip is exhausting them right now — the seat tells me the capacity is starved, not why or for how long, so 'too little' stays at what they're doing and what it takes from them. A reader could reasonably say their grip through a hard season was necessity, not a habit, and the ask must stay usable if that's true: carrying one thing without tightening around it costs nothing and needs nobody. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you started steering the room early, before anybody asked' — it guesses at history I don't have, so it goes.

attempts.check: The record says the seat is starved and that the release is late, but it does not say how long the grip has run, so I keep the cells in the present tense of what the person does and drop any duration. A reader could reasonably say their holding was what the situation demanded, not a habit, and the asks survive that: each one is small, needs nobody, and can be done badly or stopped without harm. The sentence that serves me more than them was 'held by your attention, and your attention has been paying for it' — it tells them what their energy costs before they've said it does, so it goes.
